title: We did it ourselves
hook: the best leaders are barely noticed, and people say "we did it ourselves" (Tao Te Ching 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, return to the root: everything that rises goes back, and the going back is stillness. That was your line too. Did you catch yourself rushing, and come back? Day one thousand seventy-nine.

A kid is learning to ride a bike. A parent runs alongside, one hand on the back of the seat, steadying it. Then, without saying anything, the parent lets go. The kid keeps pedaling, wobbles, steadies, and rides to the end of the street alone. At the corner, the kid turns around, beaming, and shouts: I did it! And the parent, out of breath, says: you did. Not a word about the hand on the seat. Chapter seventeen of the Tao Te Ching says that moment is what the best kind of leading looks like.
screen: `A HAND ON THE BACK OF THE SEAT.` → `THE PARENT LETS GO.` → `I DID IT!`

segments.voice: First, a ladder of leaders. The chapter ranks the ones who lead. With the best, people barely know they're there. Next, people love them and praise them. Next, people fear them. And at the bottom, people mock them. Notice where love and praise land: second, not first. A leader everyone praises is still standing in the center of the picture. The best one has stepped out of it. Second, trust. The chapter adds a short, sharp line: where there isn't enough trust, there will be no trust in return. A leader who doesn't trust people breeds people who don't trust the leader. The best leader steps back partly because they trust the people to do the work. Third, the quiet hand. The best leaders, the chapter says, are unhurried and careful with their words. They don't make speeches about what they're doing. They do what's needed and go quiet again. Fourth, the ending, which gives the chapter its name here. When the work is done and things have turned out well, the people all say: this happened by itself; we did it ourselves. The word underneath is ziran: of itself so, or natural. The chapter counts it as success when nobody gives the leader the credit. That can be a hard thing to want. But a parent, a teacher, a manager, a friend, anyone who has helped someone grow, has had the chance to be that hand on the seat: steadying, then letting go, and letting the joy belong to someone else.
screen: `THE BEST ARE BARELY NOTICED.` · `NOT ENOUGH TRUST, NO TRUST BACK.` · `UNHURRIED, CAREFUL WITH WORDS.` · `WE DID IT OURSELVES.` · then, large: `OF ITSELF, SO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help without taking credit. Settle, and bring to mind someone you could help today: a coworker stuck on something, a kid with homework, a friend making a decision. Picture helping in a way that leaves them holding the result. A question instead of an answer. A hand on the seat, then letting go. Notice whether part of you wants them to know it was you. That's all right; just notice it, and let it rest. The bell holds the time.
We did it ourselves. Chapter seventeen's sign of the best leading: the work gets done, and the people say it happened of itself. Today's word.
Your line: they did it themselves. Help one person today, then step back, and when it works out, let them have the whole of it. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 1079 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN THE WAY IS LOST.`

howItsDone: Some teachers, parents and managers who read the Tao Te Ching take chapter seventeen as a model: they help quietly and step back, so the people they help can own the result.

fork.setup: you quietly helped a friend fix a problem. now they're telling everyone, "I figured it out myself." what do you do?
options: remind them, kindly, that you helped.
let them say it, and be glad.
tell the others what really happened.
fork.reveal: in chapter seventeen, success is when the work is done and the people say, we did it ourselves.

original.note: Chinese: of itself so, natural. What the people say in chapter seventeen's last line.

trapdoor: what you thought: we did it ourselves is something people say when nobody helped.
what it means: the best leaders help so quietly that, when the work is done, the people believe they did it alone, and that counts as success.
what a scholar hears: ziran, of itself so, a word the book uses for the Tao's own way of being; here the people use it of themselves.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 25 (the Tao follows ziran)

notes: Chapter 17 paraphrased throughout (Legge's rendering of the last line was not quoted; the writer could not confirm it word for word).
The first line has textual variants: 太上，下知有之 ('the people below know they exist') versus 不知有之 ('do not know they exist'); rendered as 'barely know they're there'. Confirm.
The trust line (信不足焉，有不信焉) is read in more than one way; the teach takes it as mutual distrust. Confirm.
Trapdoor floor 3: ziran as the Tao's own way of being leans on chapter 25 (道法自然); added to sources. Confirm.
Editor pass: garbled gloss of ziran ('of itself, so of itself, natural') rewritten.
